[i]You give me fever when you kiss me, fever when you hold me tight. Fever in the morning, fever all through the night. Fever![/i] [h1]📝 Main Pros, Cons, and Suggestions:[/h1] 🟩 Pros: + Music is enjoyable + Experience and coins don’t disappear between waves + Gacha pull animation is a fun way to discover unlocks + Sector selection lets you narrow your focus (exp, coins, or specific crafts) + Crafting is a new addition to the genre, adding an additional layer to upgrade paths + The speed at which the developers addressed and corrected the bugs and concerns I initially listed is commendable (a few hours) 🟥 Cons: - Later waves were a tedious grind, but enemy health is still being adjusted - Bugs (several were fixed soon after posting this review, but some still remain) 🏷️ Suggestions: ~ Mouse aim ~ Reduce level up effects, they take up too much screen space ~ Pin crafting requirements so upgrades are marked rather than needing to memorise them ~ Ice cube gun is OP, it freezes bosses constantly, effectively making their fight risk free, consider reducing the freeze time [h1]Gachi Fever doesn't do the genre justice[/h1] Gacha Fever (GF) takes the VS like formula and flips it on its head, attempting to add additional depth while slowing the pace of play. It certainly understands what a VS like is, but does it understand what makes it good? In my short experience, yes, sort of. Crafting is an addition I enjoy as it adds another layer of depth to item selection – Do I risk it and hope RNG favours me or do I play it safe and focus on guaranteed upgrades? The red zone and end of wave upgrades, however, are something I despise. Limiting the play area via the red zone and locking weapon upgrades until a wave is completed isn’t fun – These reduce the pace of play, reducing the dopamine hit I look for from the genre. My biggest issues were how weak I felt, how spongey enemies were, and the number of bugs I faced. Since posting my initial review however, the developers promptly released a patch addressing these concerns and issues. For this reason I recommend the game - It's cheap, it's relatively fun, and the devs are quick to act. A quirky, currently slightly flawed and very cute Gatcha themed Survival Rogue-like. Overall, I have a very positive experience with this game as someone who enjoys rogue-likes with meta progression. It's design is interesting and shakes up the formula just enough to feel original in a wash of survival roguelikes. Having bested the games hardest challenge I feel I have a firm grasp on the games mechanics and I've been watchin' over this game for a few months now playing it with each patch. And right now it is in a very good spot compared to it's previous versions. But it IS lacking a few things, some of the screens are glitchy, some mechanics aren't entirely well expressed. And the controls (for at least controller) could use some refinement and room for customization. The Stats are relatively self explanatory, however some weapons simply do not interact the same with them the same as many others. Furthermore sometimes numbers are just straight up wrong. Character verity is fairly nice, and nuanced, Akimbo and Maggi feel simple to learn for Physical and Magic, while having open enough kits to expand to other builds, while later characters specialize a little heavier to fill a niche that sometimes hits, sometimes doesn't, depending on your preference (I myself can't get a head on Moon's play-style personally) Weapons feel good, some have great punch to there attacks, and there are enough options -eventually- to make any build you want. I do feel like the gacha style unlocks does kind of hamper the feeling of progress. specially since some characters core stat is entirely locked behind unlockable items (Specifically, Crafter with the Collect stat) and I personally feel like there should be more basic items for each stat, even if they turn out to be kind of trash in later runs. It is simply pure suffering to unlock the collector or the collect-bomb before hotdog, knowing full well they aren't going to be useful for a while. Furthermore, The end game feels like it's not approachable without meta unlocks like hotdog or Akimbo's headset. This however I feel is kind of the point of the games meta prog. To get stronger over time to defeat the boss. I personally do like feeling like I beat the game eventually. Even Roguelikes. Overall, the game is a great time, and with a few adjustments to the formulae, some glitch fixing, and just a bit less HP and sheer damage on the enemies (and maybe some invul time between hits). It'd be damn near perfect.

The tl;dr version is: a lot of excellent ideas and fun mechanics, but it needs a balance update so bad. Now let's expand upon these thoughts. The game is a very interesting spin on the genre, mixing in the cute world of gacha (the toys, not the videogames), without the predatory monetization aspect. The player often gets to pull these gacha balls for a variety of things, from unlocking new characters (of which there's already a lot) and weapons to gaining several perks at once within a run. Perks can even be sacrificed to build sets, netting very unique bonuses and powers. And the runs itself are pretty interesting: players need to be smart in finding optimal synergies between weapons and perks, with even damage zones and such rendering the round-based battles very chaotic and tense. It's also cool how players get to choose whether to fight in areas that get XP (useful for perks) or coins (useful to buy and upgrade weapons). Combined with a cute artstyle, clearly the core of the game works. The one major issue here is that the game's balance is all over the place. Even in some of the early rounds, the game can become mighty difficult if the player wasn't lucky enough to get the best RNG with the weapons and perks, with certain items that already seem crucial to make any meaningful progress. Most runs it's hard to even get meaningful damage into the first boss, as we're just running around trying to chip away damage at an increment that makes Dark Souls look easy. And with the aforementioned damage zones, some of which expand indefinitely and that can not be paused, the actual playable area decreases in size rapidly, easily cornering the unlucky players. Having an optimal build is crucial, but it's also luck-based to be able to get it. Even the permanent progression is a bit of mess right now, because the upgrades all cost coins, but players only keep the unspent coins from every run. This means that Gacha Fever actively discourages from spending money in runs, or at least, encourages doing a lot of "useless" grind runs just to get more cash to become more powerful in x matches. This really should never happen in a bullet heaven. In the end, I still find the core game fun, creative and enjoyable, so I'm gonna give it a thumbs up. I do plan to revisit the game in the future however, in the hope that the grindy nature, punishing difficulty and the general power creep find some much-needed improvements. Gacha Fever is a fun bullet heaven game that looks so colorful and has many things to unlock. Completion takes around 18h and the hardest achievement is to finish a run without moving. [b]Approximate amount of time to 100%:[/b] 18 hours [b]Estimated achievement difficulty:[/b] 4/10 [b]Minimum number of playthroughs needed:[/b] It is a roguelite so you play many runs, but neve have to start a new save file [b]Is there a good guide available:[/b] No, but you don't need a guide [b]Multiplayer achievements:[/b] No [b]Missable achievements:[/b] No [b]Grinding Achievements:[/b] No [b]DLC-Only achievements:[/b] No [b]Speedrun achievements:[/b] No [b]Time-gated achievements:[/b] No [b]RNG-achievements:[/b] No [b]Does difficulty affect achievements:[/b] No difficulty option [b]Unobtainable/glitched achievements:[/b] No Gacha Fever is a very colorful bullet heaven game. There are around 4 different stages with different monsters and bosses. You will choose between those based on the current bonus for each stage. For some you get more money, for others more experience and some allow you to buy items instead of weapons. It also allows you to craft items at the end of the stage if you have own the right items to make that new item. I always tried to end a run on stage that gives more money, as you need a lot of money for the upgrades. The money you use to buy weapons is the same currency to buy the upgrades. So after finishing a run, I kept playing endless mode but without buying weapons and things anymore to rank up as much gold as I could to buy new upgrades after I died. Gacha Fever has many characters you will unlock while playing and many many weapons. Most of them are good and it is nice to combine those that use the same stat so you can focus on increasing that specific stat. The only weapon I really disliked were the boxing gloves, as they warp you toward an enemy and that is just annoying. There are many areas on the gound that will hurt you and it ignores all of that and just warps you in the middle of those if the closest enemy is standing there. I love bullet heaven games, they are so addictive and you always have those small goals to work toward. However, one thing I wish that would change in this genre in general is that games don't explain themselves. For example, I thought at the end of each level you collect a bunch of money/experience that was laying on the ground. I thought it was just all of them, but I learned through the Steam forums that it is only the part that is close to you. Another thing is that the main menu of this game shows a leaderboard, and I saw myself rising on it... how I did do that...? I have no clue. A number behind my name increased but what that number represents.. I have no idea. One last thing I would love to see is controller support. I love to play this type of game with my Xbox controller and the Steam page says "partial controller support" but the game didn't recognize any inputs from my Xbox controller. The achievements in Gacha Fever are very straightforward. Beating the different bosses at least once, and getting each hero to level 70 (so for this you don't have to complete a run, just get to level 70). I would recommend farming coins very early on to buy permanent upgrades and then play on the second difficulty as that will help you to unlock more items/heroes faster. And at the end of each run, play endless mode while going for stages that give you extra money. Stop buying weapons and just farm that money ^^. The hardest achievement is the achievement "Don't move" where you can barely move, which is a challenge with all the area of effects will be laying on the ground. I did move like 2 times one step when being so close to finishing a level and just had to move out of an area of effect. This didn't lock me out of the achievement but no idea how much you're allowed to really move. BTW this achievement unlocks after finishing a run, so I thought I had failed but gladly kept standing still until I died in endless mode. If I had known it would only unlock when finishing a run I wouldn't have gone for endless mode and maybe already had it earlier but started moving again after stage 15 when it didn't unlock? I had a lot of fun playing Gacha Fever and unlocking all the achievements. It is an addictive game! I give Gacha Fever 4 out of 5 stars. A survivor game that is a bit rough around the edges. Multiple UI issues of showing the wrong items when hovering, little feedback as to how much items scale, strange item balance (all items are equal cost. Example of some items: "-2 life, +1% damage" vs "+5% damage, +3% movement speed"), and there's a gatcha option to get random items, but some items I would deem as cursed as they give huge downsides. Pencils for example give -25% damage dealt each, so you can brick a run pretty easily.

I'd like to make it clear that I vacillated between a positive and negative review, especially given that the game offers a lot of content for its low price. Unfortunately, after 7-8 hours of play, frustration set in for reasons I'll mention below, and although I tried to persevere, the game did nothing to correct the situation. The game is a "survivor-like", where you have to equip yourself with weapons and items. These items can (and must) be accumulated to form sets that consume these items (the effects disappear) to produce a new, more powerful item. A run can be summed up as defeating a few waves in a farming zone and accessing the set crafting at the end of that zone, then moving on to another zone, and so on. Crafting is limited to 3 different sets per zone, and there is a choice of 4 zones. At the end of a game, you earn xp to lvl up your account (and unlock new items, weapons and characters) as well as currency for a skill tree. At the start of the game, the choices are limited because the pool of items (and weapons) is small. That said, after several hours, especially when you reach level 30, more and more items are added and it becomes increasingly difficult to craft the sets that are useful to you, especially as the new items form new sets, but the choice of sets per zone is the same and random. I should also mention the fact that many items are very badly balanced (some with ridiculously low values, malus, or others that are too powerful and favour a particular path). So after 8-10 hours, all you'll be doing is trying to find the item you want in a huge pile of garbage. Even if you have the items, if the RNG doesn't give you the opportunity to craft the set, it's pointless. That's how the game becomes increasingly difficult, frustrating and less fun as the hours go by. Maybe I'm being too narrow-minded and tunnel-visioned about one way of playing and itemising among others? ->No, the character you choose is bound to be highly specialised in a particular path (bonus in one type, huge malus in another), and the game leaves you no choice. If you choose character A but the game only gives you items/sets B, you're out. The game does offer the choice of banning items and weapons, and banning an item that is use in a set prevents it from appearing again, but the number of ban are still too limited compared to the number of items/sets. What's more, the ban can only be applied in a run, so the game has already imposed RNG sets for the first zone before giving you the opportunity to ban them. But what about the skill tree? In a word: useless. The upgrades are too expensive and far too weak to be really useful, after 30 or 50 hours perhaps. What's more, the actual values are lower than those displayed. There's no sense of progression or power gain inherent in this type of game. Quite the opposite, in fact, and this is the first time I've seen a game that increases in difficulty and frustration by unlocking new items. Even if your run goes superbly well and you want to continue playing in infinite mode, after a certain stage (30 or 35, I don't remember), the enemies that inflicts very little dmg up to that point will suddenly cause you to lose 1/4 HP in one hit, making the slightest mistake fatal. It's really a big wall put up there for no reason, and contrary to the progressive increase in difficulty you'd expect from an infinite mode... To that, you could add a whole host of other problems (which wouldn't be a problem if the game wasn't so frustrating): -as already mentioned, the wrong values are shown in the skill tree. -numerous small bugs when playing with the mouse, clickable boxes that don't respond or with a delay. -controls not designed with the mouse in mind, especially the activatable items on which you have to click on the 1 key every 3 seconds with the same hand that is busy controlling the character. We could have used the right mouse click, which is useless. -weapons or characters that just seem too restrictive to be fun, with no powerful advantages to compensate. Notably the boxing gloves that make the character jump on enemies every few seconds with no control whatsoever, or the character that reroll your items when you pick up new ones. If there's one thing that could easily invalidate my criticism, it's the addition of an option in the codex (which lists unlocked items) to directly ban the appearance of certain items in the game. Yes, it wouldn't be balanced, but it would be a lot more fun. Maybe I'm being too hard on a small game at this price, but it's precisely because it has so much potential that I'm all the more frustrated.

Gacha Fever, developed and published by Milkshake Games, is a fast-paced, colorful roguelite shooter that combines arcade-style action with gacha-inspired progression and an energetic sense of personality. It takes the familiar twin-stick formula—moving, shooting, and dodging through waves of enemies—and infuses it with a burst of style and variety. Every element, from the weapon designs to the flashy visuals, is crafted to evoke both chaos and charm. Beneath its cute and candy-colored aesthetic lies a game that rewards reflexes, adaptability, and a taste for experimentation. It’s an experience that doesn’t aim to reinvent the genre, but instead polishes its core mechanics with humor, creativity, and accessibility. The basic premise of Gacha Fever is easy to grasp but hard to master. Players take control of a “gacha fighter,” one of several unlockable characters obtained through a randomized draw system that serves as the game’s central gimmick. Each fighter has unique abilities and weapons that alter the way battles unfold. Once in the arena, the objective is simple—survive as long as possible while mowing down waves of increasingly aggressive enemies. The game’s roguelite structure ensures that no two runs feel quite the same: players collect currency, find temporary upgrades, and craft new weapons during their sessions, only to lose them upon defeat. This constant cycle of progress and reset gives the game its addictive pull. Runs are short enough to encourage replayability, yet each one feels rewarding thanks to the rapid pace of upgrades and the sheer visual spectacle of combat. Where Gacha Fever stands out most is in its personality. The tone is playful and chaotic, leaning into absurdity with confidence. Weapons like the “Bubble Tea Cannon” or “Magic Wand” are both ridiculous and effective, firing projectiles that fill the screen with explosions of color. The arenas are compact but beautifully designed, forcing players to adapt quickly as the playable space shrinks and enemy formations grow more complex. The game keeps tension high through its unique “shrinking zone” mechanic, which gradually compresses the battlefield and demands constant movement. Combined with its responsive controls and fast animations, the result is an experience that feels constantly alive, teetering between panic and exhilaration. It’s the kind of game where you’re never more than a few seconds away from chaos, and that’s exactly where it shines. Visually, Gacha Fever is a treat. The art style is bright, sharp, and unapologetically over-the-top, embracing a mix of anime influences and arcade flair. The environments glow with pastel lighting, while enemy designs alternate between cute and menacing, maintaining the game’s whimsical yet dangerous atmosphere. Special effects—like the explosion of colors when a powerful attack lands—add to the sense of spectacle without overwhelming the player’s vision. The soundtrack complements the aesthetic perfectly, pulsing with upbeat electronic music that keeps the tempo high from start to finish. Each sound effect, from gunfire to enemy defeat chimes, is satisfying and punchy, adding weight to every action. The overall presentation is cohesive and polished, demonstrating that Milkshake Games knew exactly what kind of tone they wanted to achieve: bright, fun, and relentless. Mechanically, the game balances simplicity with strategic depth. While the core loop revolves around surviving waves and collecting power-ups, the gacha system introduces an element of unpredictability that keeps the gameplay fresh. Unlocking new fighters or weapons through the gacha pulls is both exciting and motivating, and the randomized rewards give players reasons to return for just one more round. Crafting and upgrading mid-run add another layer of progression, allowing you to shape your character’s strengths on the fly. Even though the combat can feel chaotic, there’s enough structure for players to develop strategies—choosing when to upgrade, what to fuse, and how to position themselves as the arena closes in. It’s a system that rewards adaptability rather than memorization, making every victory feel earned. However, Gacha Fever’s strengths also highlight its limits. Its design prioritizes fast, snack-sized sessions over extended depth, meaning that after several hours, players may begin to feel the repetition set in. The pool of enemies and weapons, while varied at first, can start to cycle predictably during longer play sessions. There’s no extensive progression system beyond unlocking more gacha content, so those looking for long-term investment or narrative depth may find the game lightweight. Still, this simplicity feels deliberate rather than lazy—Gacha Fever was clearly designed as a short-burst, replay-driven experience rather than an endless grind. The only real drawback lies in its longevity; its core loop is so tightly focused that it can risk feeling familiar after enough runs. Despite these minor drawbacks, Gacha Fever succeeds in delivering exactly what it promises: an energetic, stylish, and wildly entertaining arcade shooter that doesn’t take itself too seriously. It’s easy to pick up, immediately engaging, and visually delightful. The combination of roguelite progression, gacha-based character collection, and fast-paced twin-stick shooting creates a formula that’s easy to love in short bursts and rewarding to master over time. The game’s infectious energy and creativity make it stand out in a crowded field of indie shooters, and its polished presentation ensures it feels cohesive from start to finish. For players looking for a fun, visually dynamic action game that balances chaos with charm, Gacha Fever offers a thoroughly enjoyable experience that embodies its name—it’s pure, joyful madness that’s hard to put down once the fever sets in. Rating: 8/10

Let me start of with: It's fun, but Once you get into the gameplay, the core gameplay loop is pretty fun. You buy weapons, kill enemies, level up, upgrade weapons and repeat. In its core mechanics, this is just yet another Vampire Survivors clone. Or rather, this is a clone of HoloCure minus the Vtuber theme. If it's fun, then why do you not recommend the game? Thank you for asking, for starters, the mechanics are all over the place. There is no proper balancing and, based on my experiences, thus far, you can completely break your build by just min-maxing into one stat (say evade, for example). The designs, while cutesy, fit the theme of this game. No complaints there. However when it comes to some gameplay decisions, that is where this game falls short. Say you make it to a craft stage, the only place where you can sell weapons if you are unhappy with your current build, however it seems like you can only ever sell your two highest-level weapons. Usually if I'm unhappy with a weapon after trying it, I won't put any more money into it. Thus that entire feature is pointless. Then there's the decision to include enemies that leave behind damage circles so you have to watch your step. So far so good. There's yellow ones, which disappear a few seconds after you kill the enemy and then there's purple ones which STAY PERMANENTLY!. There are stages (for example the beach) where a wave of 200 enemies consists of 33% permanent damage circle enemies. So not only does the stage go smaller and smaller as time passes, those random enemies also die, leaving you with yet less space to maneuver in. And if you use guns instead of melee weapons, there could be a "do not touch" patch the size of half the circle by the time you go back over there. I also don't see the purpose of giving you other guns in the store when you're already maxed out on slots. Like.. why show me guns that I don't plan on using, just so I have to waste money on a reroll? Another asinine gimmick. **Edit01: I'm raising the score to a 5/10. The Dev is doing their best to actually listen and work with the community. But since the core issue, a necessary rebalance, is not yet done, I'll still not recommend the game.** For that and a multitude other reasons, I'm giving this game a 5 out of 10. It needs some serious polishing and re-balancing to raise that score.

Despite my enjoyment, I cannot recommend this to everyone. The major issue is the lack of maneuverability the game allows. Every level except for the beach has obstructions everywhere. You must find a way around a wall, but the enemies pass through with ease. So you can't even use the environment to your advantage. If that weren't enough, there's a red ring of death. If you go outside the ring, you get hurt. And on top of that, the ring shrinks rapidly. If these issues didn't exist, the game would be great. But I don't see these issues ever being fixed.
